ENTRY SCOPE · TENDAM · INDONESIA

Tendam’s Indonesia Roadmap

A market-entry plan for Springfield and Cortefiel — scope, economics, operator, and sequence.

A Vitrine Advisory market-entry assessment. Independent, sourced, and editorial — prepared as a point of view, not a commissioned brief. All figures verified against company filings and primary reporting, October 2026.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The verdict, in one line

THE VITRINE VIEW

Springfield has a genuine, time-sensitive opening in Indonesia — but only through a committed, capitalised master-franchise and a digital-first launch. A tentative, distributor-light entry would fade, as such entries have before. Cortefiel follows in phase two.

The case rests on a simple asymmetry. Tendam — the Madrid group behind Springfield, Cortefiel, Women'secret and Pedro del Hierro — is the strongest it has ever been, actively hunting new markets, and newly capitalised by Abu Dhabi. Yet it is absent from Indonesia, Southeast Asia's largest consumer market, while already trading next door in the Philippines. That gap is the opportunity. The risk is not the market; it is the manner of entry.

THE SITUATION

A group at full strength, with a hole in its map

Tendam (founded in Madrid in 1880; formerly Grupo Cortefiel) closed its 2025 financial year — the twelve months to 28 February 2026 — with the best numbers in its history, in its first full year under majority owner 2PointZero (the Abu Dhabi investment vehicle formerly known as Multiply Group, holding 67.9%).

The group runs nearly 2,000 points of sale across ~89 countries, and has set out an explicit ambition: to roughly double revenue to about €3bn by 2030, with ~140 new stores planned for 2026 alone — nearly triple the prior year's pace — and a target of 2,500 stores by 2030. International expansion is the stated engine.

Yet the map has a conspicuous hole. Tendam's store concentration today runs across Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, Mexico, the Middle East, North Africa and Latin America. Springfield trades in the Philippines and has built steadily in India through a master-franchise partner. Indonesia — the region's single largest market — is absent.

THE PRIZE

Why Indonesia, and why this segment

Indonesia fits Springfield's proposition with unusual precision.

The consumer wave

Indonesia's middle class is projected to reach roughly 141 million by 2030. Around 70% of the population is of productive age, and Gen-Z and millennials will be the dominant spending cohort by the end of the decade. This is a market growing into the exact consumer Springfield serves.

The positioning gap

Springfield targets the 25–35 age group with affordable, contemporary, easy-to-wear fashion. In Jakarta's mall landscape this sits in genuine white space — above the value-basics tier on design, below the premium-contemporary tier on price. It is the band where Indonesian trade-up spending is concentrating: broadly the Rp 300k–1.2m apparel range. Cortefiel, aimed at 35–45 smart-casual and tailoring, addresses a smaller but under-served professional-wardrobe segment caught between fast-fashion and hard luxury.

The fit is structural, not forced

Both brands are lightweight and trans-seasonal — no heavy-outerwear mismatch with the climate — and their tailored, layerable pieces adapt naturally to modest styling, which is an opportunity for localisation rather than a barrier.

Springfield's India trajectory — a patient, city-by-city build serving quality-seeking emerging-market youth — is a near-exact template for Indonesia. The India playbook is the Indonesia blueprint.

THE ECONOMICS

A de-risked model — if it is structured right

The franchise model is the strategic advantage, because it places almost no capital at risk for the brand owner. Under Tendam's model, the local partner owns the stores and the inventory, buys product from Tendam, and funds fit-out, staff and rent — while earning a higher mark-up than competing franchises typically offer. Tendam takes an entry fee and a wholesale margin, and supplies the brand, the merchandising system and sourcing through its established Hong Kong logistics hub — which sits logistically close to Indonesia.

There is a second structural lever: Tendam leases its brands together as a co-tenancy package — Springfield, Cortefiel and Women'secret taken as one — which spreads fixed cost and strengthens negotiating power with mall landlords. A single operator relationship can therefore carry multiple banners into the market on improving terms.

The economics work for both sides at once: incremental, low-downside international revenue for Tendam against its 2030 goal; a growing-brand portfolio at an attractive margin for the Indonesian operator. That mutual logic is precisely what makes the opportunity real rather than theoretical.

THE DECISIVE VARIABLE

Indonesia does not punish the brand. It punishes half-commitment.

This is where a market-entry decision is won or lost. Indonesia has a long record of international apparel brands that entered lightly — through under-resourced distributors or thinly-capitalised partners — and quietly faded, while the same brands committed real capital elsewhere in Asia and endured there. The pattern is consistent enough to be treated as a rule: in Indonesian fashion retail, the operator relationship decides the outcome more than the brand itself.

Tendam's own earlier franchise presence in Indonesia, dating to the 1990s–2000s, lapsed for exactly this reason — entry without sustained commitment. The lesson is not that the brands failed to resonate, but that light entries wither regardless of brand strength.

ROUTES TO MARKET, RANKED
RoutePartner profileThe Vitrine read
A — Established multi-brand operator A large Indonesian lifestyle-retail group with mall access and a 150-plus brand portfolio in exactly this tier. Recommended. The scale, mall relationships and multi-brand machinery de-risk the entry and suit the co-tenancy model.
B — Up-market lifestyle operator A growing portfolio house moving into accessible-premium. Viable, particularly for Cortefiel's professional positioning.
C — Dedicated regional master-franchisee A focused SEA franchise specialist, as used in India. Clean and proven — contingent on securing the right partner.

THE RECOMMENDED PLAY

Phased, and digital-first from day one

Year 1 — Prove it (2–3 doors)

A Springfield anchor store in a young, high-traffic, mid-market mall — a Grand Indonesia or a Central Park, deliberately not a top-luxury centre, which is the wrong consumer. One Cortefiel test unit in a professional-skewing mall. Critically, a TikTok Shop and Tokopedia presence from launch — this is non-negotiable. Indonesia is the world's second-largest social-commerce market; a mall-only entry would ignore where discovery and purchase now happen, and would repeat the historic error.

Year 2 — Expand on validation (4–6 doors)

Deepen in Jakarta and extend to Surabaya and Bandung; fold Women'secret into the co-tenancy package to improve economics.

Year 3 — Scale (10–15 points of sale)

With digital treated as a co-equal channel rather than an afterthought.

THE VERDICT

Conviction, and a condition

SPRINGFIELD — ENTER, WITH CONDITIONS · CONVICTION: HIGH

Tendam's strength, capital and mandate align with Indonesia's largest-in-region consumer growth at a live moment — and the brand's own emerging-market playbook already works. The window is open while the group is actively expanding. The condition precedent is commitment: a first-rank master-franchise and a digital-first launch. Structured that way, Springfield can repeat India. Structured half-way, it repeats the retreats of the past.

Cortefiel — Watch, phase two. The under-served professional segment is real, but lower volume and zero awareness make it the second move. It should enter on Springfield's co-tenancy coattails, once the operator relationship is proven.
